meaningMnemonic: This is the call radical. Do you see how it looks like an old-timey phone with the handset on top? "Nothing better than a phone for making a call," as my dad used to say.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means exit .
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means farming .
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means peoples .
Do you see the slightly weird looking rake ? It's lying on the floor, waiting to be used.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means substitute .
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means surplus .

A woman sitting on a stool with a broken heart is very angry . She had her heart broken by some jerk and now she’s sitting on the stool, just stewing over the guy and how angry she is with him. Hints This woman is so angry! Pretend you are the woman. Sit on your stool and feel your heart, painful in your chest, as you fume and think about how angry you are.
readingMnemonic: The woman feels so angry that she decides to sic her do g ( ど ) on the guy who broke her heart. That ought to teach him — there's nothing worse than getting chased by an angry woman's angry dog. Hints Imagine the woman's angry dog running around and barking at the guy as he tries to escape, all while the woman watches from her stool. She's still angry too, but she's starting to feel a little better about everything.

meaningMnemonic: You want to go to the sun so you set up a slide twenty stories tall so you can ascend into the heavens. Hints Feel the air whoosh past your face as you shoot off the end of the long slide and ascend into the air. It's starting to get hot and the sun is getting closer!
readingMnemonic: You need to ascend into the sky and toward the sun because the Shou gun ( しょう ) said so. He's testing out some space travel technology (the twenty story slide) and you're his guinea pig. Hints As you ascend, look back through tear-filled eyes and see the Shougun staring up at you. He nods slightly. You've pleased him.

meaningMnemonic: If you're riding your scooter through some rice , it's likely you've gone astray . Also you might be lost . Hints Usually there aren't paved areas inside areas of rice. You must be really lost if you ended up here with your scooter.
readingMnemonic: You got so lost and went so astray you ended up on the May flower  ( めい ), a ship that eventually took you across the Atlantic Ocean. Now you've really, really gone astray. Hints How you got so lost that you ended up on an old ship from 1620 is beyond my understanding. But you did it.

meaningMnemonic: Someone is reaching out with their fingers to call for you. They beckon you closer, this way. Hints Something about the way they're beckoning you with their fingers is really enticing. You can't help but walk toward them.
readingMnemonic: The person beckon ing you is the Shou gun ( しょう ). You can't help but obey the Shougun's beckoning call. Hints Even if the Shougun didn't have an army that would crush you if you didn't come when he called, you'd go anyway. Those beckoning fingers are just so... weirdly enticing.

meaningMnemonic: After a tsunami hit your farming land, you're gonna see a lot of dense silt left behind. This thick layer really enriches the soil, and your crops will come out tasting extra thick and dense in flavor. Hints Imagine your farming land absolutely covered with this dense layer of silt from the tsunami, but then seeing your crops sprouting up one after another, thicker than ever. It’s all very thick and dense, we think you get the point.
readingMnemonic: Know who’s likely responsible for this dense , thick layer of silt? No stradamus ( のう ). He’s the one who urged you to buy this farmland in the first place, likely because he predicted the tsunami would bring this thick layer of silt. Hints You can always rely on Nostradamus’ predictions hitting the mark, even when it comes to thickly-layered-silt-bringing tsunamis. Good ol’ reliable Nostradamus.

meaningMnemonic: When your eye s get droopy , it means you're getting drowsy . Go get some shut-eye, you droopy-eyed drowsy person. Hints You're so drowsy that your eyelids have drooped all the way down to the floor. Be careful not to step on them as you drowsily make your way to bed.
readingMnemonic: The reason you're so drowsy is because you're on a swing ( すい ). A swing works like a baby cradle — it rocks you and makes you feel drowsy right away! Hints Feel yourself getting drowsier and drowsier as the swing gently rocks you to sleep. Hopefully it's one of those swings with the leg holes so you don't fall out as you're drifting off.

meaningMnemonic: Under a canopy supported by a stick , Wolverine is sipping some water and relaxing. He looks so at ease and at peace . Hints The stick-supported canopy is basically a beach parasol, and Wolverine is absolutely radiating vibes of ease and peace as he sips his water beneath it.
readingMnemonic: Together with Wolverine in this place of ease and peace , you also spot こう いち . He's hanging out under the canopy and sipping water too. Hints こういち sees you and invites you to come under the canopy with him and Wolverine. Why not? You could use some ease and peace in your life.

meaningMnemonic: Setting up a stand on the top of a mountain , you rake all the rocks to the edge of it. You want to clear the area around your stand, so you get your rake out and you rake all the stones and debris away from the stand and toward the edge of the mountain top. It also creates a small barrier around the edge as well. Hints Imagine yourself at the top of the mountain, holding the rake in your hands. Look over the edge. Feel the sinking feeling in your stomach as you realize how high up you really are.
readingMnemonic: You set up this stand at the top of the mountain so you could give a speech to the world. But you need to look your best, so you decide to get a tan ( たん ). You lie next to the edge of the mountain, and prepare to tan. Everyone likes a person with a healthy tan. Hints Imagine yourself at the edge of this mountain getting your tan on. Feel the sun beating down on you and feel the fresh mountain breeze blowing over your body. It’s very relaxing.

meaningMnemonic: There aren't many tree s in your under ground prison , so you've been given a task: using only your mouth and a stool , plant as many in the ground as you can. It's an extreme challenge! Hints How are you going to approach this weirdly specific, extreme task? Dig a hole using the stool and then plant the trees with your mouth? Good luck figuring this one out! You're in a weird underground prison for a reason, after all.
readingMnemonic: This extreme challenge could only be solved by one person: Goku ( ごく ) from Dragon Ball Z! He has a special cloak that'll allow you to plant trees in record time, so he quickly cloaks you ( きょく ) to help with your extreme task. Hints Goku barely manages to cloak you before the prison guards realize what's going on. With this cloak, you'll be planting trees with your mouth and stool like no one else before! Hooray!

meaningMnemonic: In the capital , even a broken dog can get a position . That's because the capital has so many jobs available that even a poor, broken dog can find a place to work. Hints Imagine this dog going to the capital and getting a position. The poor dog looks pretty messed up though. The radical for dog in this kanji is a bit modified, so just remember that the dog in this story is all messed up.
readingMnemonic: In order to help the dog get a position , the capital cobbler made him a pair of nice shoe s ( しゅう ). The shoes help him walk on his hurt legs, but more importantly, they boost his confidence and make him feel ready for any position. Hints Watch the broken dog settle in to his new shoes in his new home in the capital. The old dog can finally enjoy life!

meaningMnemonic: Inside the " Good Building " there's a single guy . Hints Feel free to walk around the Good Building. There are no things or people, except for that one guy. Who is that guy.
readingMnemonic: You talk to that guy . The only thing he does is offer you roe ( ろう ). Hints You try to talk to the guy, poke him, and even yell at him. But, all he does is hand you some fish roe. When you take it, he offers you more fish roe. What's up with this guy?

meaningMnemonic: The leader of your yoga class uses a special brush to stay healthy . She rubs the brush on her long arms and legs, and she never ever gets sick. Hints If you want to be healthy too, just do yoga and rub this healthy brush all over your bod.
readingMnemonic: Not everyone wants to be healthy , but Ken ( けん ) the samurai sure does. He needs to be ready at a moment's notice so he can do tasks for other people. He's at every class, rubbing himself down with the brush. Hints Imagine Ken, the picture of samurai health, doing yoga and getting that brush all up in those bits.

meaningMnemonic: You say you've left some grain on the stairs . This is how you invite people into your place. Hints Picture yourself saying out loud how you've left grain on the stairs, trying to lure people in. You're surprised people are actually falling for this.
readingMnemonic: You've invite d people in by leaving grain on the stairs but some you ths ( ゆう ) have ended up eating all the grain. Hints Imagine the youths just loitering in the stairs having eaten all the grain and taking up all the space making it impossible for anyone else to come in.

meaningMnemonic: You substitute some shellfish for collateral so your friend will lend you some money. Normally he would ask for something more valuable, but you’ve convinced him to substitute these shellfish for what he would normally take as collateral when lending to people. Hints "Shellfish used to be money! People used to lend them to each other all the time!" you say to your friend. "Hmm... okay, I guess so," they say skeptically.
readingMnemonic: You want your friend to lend you some money so you can buy yourself a ca r ( か ). You need money and a car a lot more than you need this pile of shellfish, so you’re happy to put them up as collateral for the loan. Hints Imagine yourself in this new car that you got with the money your friend lent you. Hear the roar of the engine and feel the wind in your hair.

meaningMnemonic: Your soul stand s in the village you long for . It's the village you're from, and no matter how far you go, no matter how old you get, your soul is still there, and you yearn for it. Hints Have you ever been away from your village? Maybe you're far away right now, studying Japanese alone. Can't you feel your body longing for your soul back home?
readingMnemonic: No matter how much you long for it, you can't go back because a cougar ( あこが ) is in the way. Whenever you try to return to your village to be reunited with the soul you yearn for, a cougar is back, and won't let you in. Hints You long for a cougar to leave you alone! You yearn for a cougar to bother someone else!

meaningMnemonic: A drunkard who has his mouth on the ground , has a heart that is misguided . First of all, he tries to drink his problems away, but worse, he's so drunk he's trying to drink out of the ground. Hints Picture this misguided drunkard. His whole deal is messed up.
readingMnemonic: Nowadays we don't say misguided , we say wack ( わく ). Like, damn that drunkard is so messed up, he's wack. Hints Did I do it? Did I figure out the kid lingo? Am I cool? Or am I just another wack, misguided adult?

meaningMnemonic: If you're on your scooter and you run over a root , you'll need to retreat . The roots have obviously reject ed you, they want you to leave, so you should. Hints Picture the roots raising up a little bit from the ground and tripping up your scooter. They reject you, so you should just retreat.
readingMnemonic: You're trying to retreat by scooting backwards, but the roots grab onto your tie ( たい ). You try to pull your tie off but it's just getting tighter and tighter around your neck. Hints You didn't retreat fast enough, the roots are rejecting your life, and strangling you with your own tie.

meaningMnemonic: When you ride a scooter you'll have a surplus of possible route s. Not only can you drive on any road, but you can ride on the sidewalk too! Hints Okay, so it might not be legal to take the sidewalk route depending on where you live, but physically, you can do whatever you want because scooters are small.
readingMnemonic: You decide to take the fastest route , since you have so many options, and drive on the sidewalk. However, in doing so you run over every single toe ( と ) on every single person trying to walk there. Hints Psh, whatever. They aren't your toes, and this is the fastest route! You'll name it the toe route and do whatever you want.

meaningMnemonic: Closing each eye is something that the peoples do before they sleep . The peoples can’t sleep with both eyes open and they can’t sleep with just one eye open either. Peoples have to close each eye before they can sleep. Hints You are one of these peoples, so imagine yourself closing your eyes and sleeping. Go ahead and do it right now. Close one eye, and then the other. Now imagine yourself sleeping.
readingMnemonic: The reason you want to sleep is because all the other peoples were mean ( みん ) to you. They were so mean that the only way you could get over it was to close your eyes and sleep. You just want to sleep. Hints Those other peoples were really mean to you. Imagine all the mean things they were saying to you. What did they say? Think about all these mean things as you close your eyes and drift off to sleep. Also keep in mind that this kanji has the same reading as 民 , which is included in this kanji.

meaningMnemonic: In the sun while holding a comb in a cage and sitting on a stool , you comb your hair in your spare time . Since you’re in a cage, you actually fashioned this comb yourself, so it’s a little messed up, missing a prong. You’re working on improving it in your spare time, and you also use it to style your mop. Hints Imagine yourself in your spare time, sitting on this stool in a cage in the sun. Feel the warmth of the sun on your body and feel the metal bars of the cage holding you in. You try to forget about your situation by combing your hair with the comb. The comb radical is a little modified, so be sure to remember that you made this comb yourself and it’s a little wonky.
readingMnemonic: So how did you get in this cage? Well, before you used to comb your hair in your spare time , you used to steal ca rs ( か ). You’d stolen many a car in your day, but you finally got caught in the act of stealing a car, and now you’re spending all of your spare time in that cage, just combing your hair. Hints Picture yourself in this cage. You’re going to be there for life because you’d stolen too many cars. Feel the tears run down your face as you continue to comb your hair. You’re going to die in this cage.

meaningMnemonic: Cut this comb up with your weapon and turn it into the steps for some stairs . Hints When you think about it, a comb is like a ladder. So if you cut all the rungs off with your weapon and put them on the ground, they turn into stairs!
readingMnemonic: You slowly work to create these stairs , you have to slice up a lot of combs, and at dawn ( だん ) they are done! Hints Imagine standing at the top of the stairs you made yourself, looking down at the entire town below you, as the light of dawn breaks and fills everything before you with light. And now more people can see this beautiful sight if they climb your steps.

meaningMnemonic: When someone is sick in order to diagnose the correct cause and treatment, you need to check their symptom s. You have to be especially careful too, because if you get a symptom wrong, you could kill them! Hints If you know all of the symptoms for each and every sickness you'd be able to cure them all!
readingMnemonic: You need to figure out the symptom s the Shou gun ( しょう ) is having. This is really serious too, so you better be correct about which sickness he has. If something bad happens to the Shougun it will be off with your head. Hints You get all up close and personal with the Shougun. Hmm, his symptoms are watery eyes, stuffy nose, angry shouting (wait no, that's not a symptom, is it?). Don't mess up!

meaningMnemonic: You pull on a thread as you stand with a towel wrapped around you. This allows you to tighten the towel. Hints Imagine pulling this thread and feeling your towel tighten around you. It's getting so tight that you can barely stand properly, which is probably why the stand radical looks a little weird here.
readingMnemonic: You're tighten ing your towel because you've been eating a lot of ta ter ( てい ) tots lately. You want to keep a slim figure, and rather than give up your beloved tater tots, you've just opted to constrict yourself with this towel, corset-style. Hints You really don't need to do this, you know — eating tater tots isn't a sin. Tighten that towel just enough to be snug and comfy, and keep enjoying your taters. No one's judging you.

meaningMnemonic: The scooter is white . This color will urge and compel you to use it. Scooter companies use colors to get you to do what they want. Some would say they are trying to coerce you, even. Hints Look at how white the scooter is. It urges you to use it. It compels you. You feel coerced...
readingMnemonic: When they urge , compel and coerce you like this, they are hack ing ( はく ) your brain. Hints Really all marketing, advertising, and the like is just a hack of your brain. Hint: If you see 白 in a kanji, there's a good likelihood the reading will be はく .

meaningMnemonic: Someone just asked you to say which direction they should visit . Hints You better think long and hard about where you think they should visit before you say so. They're relying on you.
readingMnemonic: You end up saying, "You should visit my ho me ( ほう )." How kind of you! Hints Your home is just over that direction, and it's your favorite place to visit, so why wouldn't this stranger want to visit your home too?! So come and visit my home, random person!

meaningMnemonic: Taking a thread and moving to the sound of the music, a drunkard makes a weave through some fabric. He’s using the thread to weave his clothes back together after he damaged them in a fall down the stairs. You know, because he’s a drunkard. Hints Imagine this drunkard bipping and bopping to the sound of the music as he weaves this thread through his clothes to repair them.
readingMnemonic: This drunkard is really chic ( しき ), but he's just fallen on hard times and has been hitting the bottle pretty hard lately. The piece of clothing he's using the thread to weave back together is one of his fancy chic outfits. Hints Imagine this drunkard, and his chic but shabby appearance. Let's hope he can repair that chic outfit and go back to being his usual chic self.

meaningMnemonic: If your soul is lying in the grass in a treasure chest , you're going to worry about it. It's just sitting there, out in the open, waiting for anyone to come and open it. Hints Picture your soul curled up inside this treasure chest that's just sitting out on the grass. Anyone could open it up and look inside, and this worries you quite a bit!
readingMnemonic: Unfortunately, you also worry about opening it yourself. You stand in front of the chest and think, "Should I open it? Nah, yah ( なや ). Wait. Nah. Yah. Dang, you can't make up your mind. Hints You worry about what you'll find if you look directly at your soul. But you also worry about what will happen if someone else looks. So you're stuck in a constant state of worrying: nah or yah?!

meaningMnemonic: You see a flag by the exit letting you know to yield . There’s cross traffic just outside the exit, and the flag lets you know that you need to yield to them. Hints Look at this flag telling you to yield. Now look through the exit right by the flag. You can see a bunch of people out there walking. Imagine standing by the exit, yielding to the other people until you have an opening. Hear the hustle and bustle of the people as you wait.
readingMnemonic: Even though the flag told you to yield , you’re starting to lose your patience. The people walking outside the exit are all a bunch of crazy old coots ( くつ )! These crazy coots keep walking right in front of the door, getting in the way. The old coots aren’t even going anywhere, they just keep looping around to obstruct the way! Hints Darn coots! Forget the yield flag, it’s time to exit. Imagine busting out of the exit, punching and pushing your way through the old coots. Hear them scream and shout “Augh! My hip!” as you plow through them.

meaningMnemonic: A healthy bit of forget ting symptom s means you might have amnesia . 健忘症 often refers to short-term memory loss , either full or partial, but some people might also use it in a sort of joking way for everyday forgetfulness .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 健忘症は不治の病なんでしょうか。
sentences.english: Is amnesia an incurable disease?

sentences.japanese: 去年、有田さんは一過性の健忘症になってしまった。
sentences.english: Last year, Mr. Arita suffered from transient amnesia.

sentences.japanese: お医者さんに健忘症の疑いがあると言われました。
sentences.english: The doctor told me that he suspected amnesia.

sentences.japanese: 健忘症に苦しんでいる親戚がいます。
sentences.english: I have a relative who is suffering from amnesia.

meaningMnemonic: You've take n a decision from someone. By doing this, you've created a kind of arrangement with them. Imagine yourself pulling this decision out of the person. They don't want to necessarily give it to you, but they're letting you pull it out of them, kind of. When you've pulled it out, you've come to an arrangement, though they've pulled some of your decision out too.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading for both kanji, which you might have guessed already since there's hiragana sticking out of both of them. The 取り comes from 取る and the 決め comes from 決める . Put them together and what have you got? Bibbidi bobbidi とりきめ !

sentences.japanese: ちゃんと取り決めを守ってもらえるのか、不安です。
sentences.english: I'm worried about whether they'll obey the agreement.

sentences.japanese: ルームメイトと生活上の取り決めをしておいた方がいいよ。
sentences.english: You should make living arrangements with your roommate.

sentences.japanese: サーモンさんと我が社で取り交わした契約によると、残念なことに彼女が競合他社のCMに出演することについて我々は何の取り決めも行っておりませんでした。
sentences.english: According to the contract between our company and Ms. Salmon, it is unfortunate, but we did not make an agreement regarding her appearance in our competitor’s commercials.

meaningMnemonic: You visit someone (or somewhere) with a question in mind. This is a visit . Any proper visit tries to answer a question, right? Like, "How have you been?" or "What kind of place is this?" If there's no question behind your visit, you're kind of just wandering around. 訪問 is a somewhat formal word for visiting somewhere or calling on someone, so you'll most often encounter it in writing or conversations in business or professional contexts.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: この間の訪問の際、何かお気に触るようなことをしてしまいましたか？
sentences.english: Is there something that got on your nerves when I visited you the other day?

sentences.japanese: もうちょっと安い訪問サービスはないんですか？
sentences.english: Don't you have a home-visit care service that is a bit cheaper?

sentences.japanese: 家庭訪問は、先生が生徒の家庭を訪ね、家庭環境を観察し、保護者と話すためのものです。
sentences.english: Home visits are for teachers to visit students' homes, observe the home environment, and have conversations with parents.

sentences.japanese: 日本では、通常歯医者に一回の訪問で治療を済ませてもらうことはできません。
sentences.english: In Japan, you usually can't get all your dental treatment done in just one visit.

meaningMnemonic: This is the noun version of worry , making it a worry , or a trouble .
readingMnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji. Nicely done, no need to have a worry about it.

sentences.japanese: あんたは何の悩みもなさそうでいいよね。
sentences.english: You seem like you don't have any worries at all, huh? That must be nice.

sentences.japanese: ストッキングがすぐに伝線しちゃうのが悩みなんです。
sentences.english: I've been bothered by how easily my stockings get runs.

sentences.japanese: 昔は悩みを人に打ち明けることができないのが悩みでしたが、今では何でも言えるようになりました。
sentences.english: In the past, my concern was not being able to confide in others, but now I can talk about anything.

sentences.japanese: 悩み事の相談に乗るのは構わないんだけど、金欠なんだよね。外食したいなら、あんたの奢りだよ。
sentences.english: I don't mind hearing about your troubles, but I'm running out of money. If you want to eat out with me, it's your treat.

meaningMnemonic: 影響 is "influence," so an evil influence is a bad influence .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: あの男がみんなに悪影響を与えたんだよ。
sentences.english: That man was a bad influence on all of us.

sentences.japanese: 悪影響が自分の子どもにまで及んでいたことに気が付き、彼女は泣き出した。
sentences.english: She cried as she realized that her bad influence filtered down to her children.

sentences.japanese: YouTubeは便利だけど、子供に悪影響が出そうな動画もあるから注意が必要だよね。
sentences.english: YouTube is convenient, but we need to be careful because some videos may be harmful to children.

sentences.japanese: スマホが人類にもたらした悪影響は計り知れないと思うよ。
sentences.english: I think the negative impact that smartphones have had on humanity is immeasurable.

meaningMnemonic: Ugh, that field guy . He's the worst. Always in the fields, making us look bad, quite the bastard . Really though, he's just this guy, but for some reason I sometimes don't like him. While 野郎 can be a casual term for a man, it's usually used to insult or show annoyance towards someone. So it's best to avoid using it unless you're really sure it's okay!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: あの野郎の物の言い方が気に入らねぇんだよ。
sentences.english: I just don't like the way that bastard speaks.

sentences.japanese: パーティーでは野郎どもがどんちゃんさわぎをしていた。
sentences.english: The guys were making a ruckus at the party.

sentences.japanese: この野郎、よくもやったな！
sentences.english: You rascal, how dare you!

sentences.japanese: あのクソ野郎がセールス・マネージャーに昇進するなんて本当に気に食わねぇ。
sentences.english: That bastard got promoted to sales manager. I’m sick to my stomach.

meaningMnemonic: I retreat ! I yield ! I can't take it anymore, it's so boring . Just imagine yourself giving up on whatever you're doing because you're so darn bored. You can't stand it. You have to retreat. You are ready to yield. Booooooring.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: ケガのせいで外出もできなかったので、かなり退屈な一週間でした。
sentences.english: I couldn't even go out because of the injury, it was such a boring week.

sentences.japanese: 退屈していたのでちょうどよかったです。
sentences.english: I was bored, so it was good timing.

sentences.japanese: 最近、仕事が単調になっちゃって、すごく退屈なんだよ。
sentences.english: Lately, my work has become monotonous and I'm very bored.

sentences.japanese: 果てしなく続く空の下で、生徒たちは果てしなく長くて退屈な校長の話を聞かなくてはならなかった。
sentences.english: Beneath the endless sky, students had to listen to the principal’s endless and boring speech.

meaningMnemonic: When you divide and untie things, you're unraveling the connections between them. In other words, you're doing a breakdown or dismantling of something.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: アルコールの分解を進めてくれます。
sentences.english: It promotes the breakdown of alcohol.

sentences.japanese: 小さいころ、よく時計を分解してあそんでいました。
sentences.english: When I was little, I would play with watches by disassembling them.

sentences.japanese: お父さん、電気分解の分解効率を向上させることはできる？
sentences.english: Dad, can you improve the decomposition efficiency of electrolysis?

meaningMnemonic: Coins? Bills? Both can be replace d if you want to change money at this money exchange . Just don’t do your currency exchange at the airport — the rates aren’t so great. You'll probably see this word the most in arcades where you can go to the 両替 machine and get coins to feed your crane game addiction.
readingMnemonic: The reading here is a bit weird. Instead of just being か (it changes to が for the rendaku), it is がえ . Just think that if you want change exchanged, I'm your guy ( がえ ).

sentences.japanese: UFOキャッチャーしたいのに、両替機が見つからない。
sentences.english: I want to play UFO catcher, but I can't find a change machine.

sentences.japanese: この一万円札を千円札に両替してもらえませんか？
sentences.english: Could you exchange this 10,000 yen bill for 1,000 yen bills?

sentences.japanese: すみません、両替はお断りしているんです。
sentences.english: Sorry, I’m afraid we don’t break bills.

sentences.japanese: 後で、今日習った日本語での両替の仕方について復習したいと思います。
sentences.english: I’ll review today’s lesson about how to exchange money in Japanese later.

sentences.japanese: 関西空港で両替しようと思ったんですが、両替所がしまっていました。
sentences.english: I wanted to exchange money at Kansai Airport, but the exchange counter was closed.

meaningMnemonic: You know how 替える is "to replace"? Well, you're replacing what you wear . That's a change of clothes , or spare clothes .
readingMnemonic: The reading is 着る and 替える put together. The か goes to が .

sentences.japanese: 母は、私の着替えを持ってくるのを忘れた事を謝りました。
sentences.english: My mother apologized for forgetting to bring me a change of clothes.

sentences.japanese: パジャマにお着替えする時間だよー！
sentences.english: It's time to change into your pajamas!

sentences.japanese: 今うちの息子イヤイヤ期だからお着替えするだけでも一苦労だよ。
sentences.english: My son is going through the "terrible twos" right now, so even just changing his clothes is a big pain.

sentences.japanese: もちろん子供の着替えは持ってきていたけど、まさか自分の着替えが必要になるとは思ってもいなかったから、ウォルマートで買う羽目になったよ。
sentences.english: Of course I brought a change of clothes for the kids, but I didn't expect to need a change of clothes for myself, so I had to buy some at Wal-Mart.

meaningMnemonic: You learned that 掛かる can mean "to be hooked." If you're doing something physical like climbing and your hand hooks onto something, that thing is called a handhold . Figuratively, this can also mean clue , since a clue is something you grasp onto, much like a handhold, to help you progress in solving a crime or mystery. This figurative use of 手掛かり is actually the most common!
readingMnemonic: The reading is 手 plus 掛かる put together. Just watch out for that rendaku.

sentences.japanese: 手掛かりはまだ見つからないのですか。
sentences.english: Still can't find any clues?

sentences.japanese: 今は全力で、問題解決の糸口となるような手掛かりを探しています。
sentences.english: We are currently searching wholeheartedly for clues that will lead us to a solution.

sentences.japanese: 警察は消えたベーコンの謎について何か手掛かりを見つけましたか？
sentences.english: Have the police found any clues regarding the mystery of the vanishing bacon?

sentences.japanese: 藤川さんの発言が、犯人のトリックを見抜く手掛かりになりました。
sentences.english: Mr. Fujikawa's statement provided a clue to the culprit's trickery.

meaningMnemonic: You learned that 抜ける is "to fall out." If your waist falls out, you can't remain standing. You have to curl up on the ground, like a coward .
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, which you've learned already. Go you!

sentences.japanese: 私は腰抜けだから言い返したくても言い返せないの。
sentences.english: I am such a coward, so I can't talk back even if I wanted to.

sentences.japanese: 次にオレを腰抜けと呼んだら、許さないぞ！
sentences.english: The next time you call me a coward, I will not forgive you!

sentences.japanese: 腰抜け共に何を言われても痛くもかゆくもないよ。
sentences.english: It doesn't bother me one bit what those cowards say.

sentences.japanese: 管理職に昇進する前に辞職する腰抜け社員が多すぎる。
sentences.english: There are too many coward employees who resign before being promoted to management.

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning it's probably an adjective. The kanji means dense , and this can also mean dense or thick in some contexts, like if you’re describing fog, or body hair! More generally, it can be used for anything that’s highly concentrated, so you can use it for things like deep colors, or strong coffee too!
readingMnemonic: What’s the most dense thing you can think of? A 子 ( こ ). Children are so full of joy, you can practically see how dense, thick and concentrated the joy is.

sentences.japanese: メイクが濃い
sentences.english: to have heavy make-up

sentences.japanese: 体毛が濃い
sentences.english: the body hair is thick

sentences.japanese: 内容が濃い
sentences.english: the content is rich

sentences.japanese: 味が濃い
sentences.english: the flavor is strong

sentences.japanese: 色が濃い
sentences.english: the color is dark

sentences.japanese: 濃い内容
sentences.english: rich in content

sentences.japanese: 濃い味
sentences.english: strong flavor

sentences.japanese: 濃い色
sentences.english: dark color

sentences.japanese: あ、味付け、ちょっと濃いかも。ごめんね！
sentences.english: Oh, I might have seasoned it a bit strong. Sorry!

sentences.japanese: そのメイク、濃くない？
sentences.english: Isn't that makeup too heavy?

sentences.japanese: この濃い毛をそるのに特注のカミソリが必要なんです。
sentences.english: I need a special-ordered razor in order to shave this thick hair.

sentences.japanese: 私は彼の髪は濃い紫色にしようかなって思ってるんだよね。
sentences.english: I’m thinking of dyeing his hair a deep purple.

meaningMnemonic: When something is dense to a certain degree , you’re talking about the density or concentration of something.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: この、マンモグラフィ濃度って何ですか？
sentences.english: What is this mammographic density?

sentences.japanese: これは濃度20%の食塩水です。
sentences.english: This is a saline solution with a concentration of 20%.

sentences.japanese: 市販のタイカレーペーストは、高濃度の塩分を含んでいるのであまり好きじゃありません。
sentences.english: Store-bought Thai curry paste contains high concentrations of salt, so I don't like it.

sentences.japanese: あなたの血中アルコール濃度については追って連絡致します。
sentences.english: I’ll get back to you on your blood-alcohol concentration.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 構う is "to care about"? You can convert it into お構いなく to politely tell someone not to care about you. So this means, don't mind me . It can also mean without regard for , especially when someone keeps doing something without caring about other people, their surroundings, or unfavorable conditions.
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 構う , so if you know that you know this!

sentences.japanese: すぐ帰りますので、お構いなく。
sentences.english: I'll get going soon so please don't mind me.

sentences.japanese: うちの家のことは、どうかお構いなく。自分たちでなんとかしますから。
sentences.english: Please don't worry about us. We will take care of it ourselves.

sentences.japanese: 社長がOKと言おうが言うまいが、お構いなく話は進んだ。
sentences.english: The discussion proceeded without any regard to whether the president gave his approval or not.

sentences.japanese: 「コーヒーはいかがですか？」「いえ、結構です。お構いなく。」
sentences.english: ”Would you like some coffee?" “No, thank you. Don’t worry about me.”

sentences.japanese: 見てるだけなので、お構いなく。
sentences.english: I'm just looking, so don't mind me.

meaningMnemonic: Remember 頑張る means “to persevere” or “to do one’s best”? This time you're telling someone to 頑張る , so this word means something like do your best , hang in there , or good luck ! Speaking of which, 頑張れ , you!
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 頑張る . Just watch out for that rendaku on 張る ! You've seen it before, but here's a mnemonic in case you need a refresher: Remember how when it's time to 頑張る (to persevere), you always scream "baa"? Not sure why, but it's a great motivator for you. So you do the same when you cheer for others. When you tell them Do your best , you also scream baa ( ば ) at them. When you tell them Hang in there , you scream "baa!" If it makes you persevere, it must work the same for others, right? Baa!

sentences.japanese: 頑張れニッポン、負けるなニッポン！
sentences.english: Do your best Japan! Hang in there Japan!

sentences.japanese: 大丈夫だって。春ちゃんならきっと受かるよ。頑張れ。
sentences.english: You'll be fine, Haru-chan. I'm sure you'll pass the test. Good luck!

sentences.japanese: 頑張れ、あとちょっとで助けが来るぞ！
sentences.english: Hang in there, help is almost here!

sentences.japanese: まあ、結果を気にせずに、頑張れよ！
sentences.english: Well, don’t worry about the results, just try your best!

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This refers to a literal edge, not a figurative one. 端 refers to the edge or end of something, like the edge of a table, the far end of a bridge, or even the corner of a page.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: If you're on edge , just eat some hash ( はし ) browns to feel better! And if you're going to the edge of the world, hash browns will probably help you make it there too. Hash browns are so useful!

sentences.japanese: このテーブルの端とそっちのテーブルの端をくっつけてください。
sentences.english: Please put the edge of this table and the edge of that table together.

sentences.japanese: どうして日本人は電車の席の端から座っていくんですか。
sentences.english: Why do Japanese people start sitting from the end of the row of train seats?

sentences.japanese: この本は、端から端まで何度も読んだので、内容は全て暗記しています。
sentences.english: I've read this book from cover to cover many times, so I have memorized all of its content.

sentences.japanese: 私は大粒の涙がコウイチの目の端からこぼれ落ちるのを見てしまった。
sentences.english: I saw a big teardrop falling from the corner of Koichi's eye.

meaningMnemonic: For year s and years, your comrade s have been with you, but now they're all elderly . This is a less common version of 年配 , but you'll still sometimes encounter it.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. As this vocab is identical to 年配 , it's also read the same. Just remember that the はい turns into ぱい !

sentences.japanese: 年輩の人
sentences.english: an elderly person

sentences.japanese: 年輩の女性
sentences.english: an elderly woman

sentences.japanese: 年輩の男性
sentences.english: an elderly man

sentences.japanese: 年輩の方々
sentences.english: elderly people

sentences.japanese: ご年輩
sentences.english: elderly

sentences.japanese: 年輩者
sentences.english: an elder

sentences.japanese: 年輩層
sentences.english: elderly population, older generation

sentences.japanese: 年輩社員
sentences.english: senior employees

sentences.japanese: このカフェは年輩の方に人気だそうです。
sentences.english: Apparently, this café is popular with the older crowd.

sentences.japanese: となりの席では、ご年輩の女性が一人でコーヒーを飲んでいらっしゃいました。
sentences.english: Next to me, an elderly woman was drinking coffee by herself.

sentences.japanese: 事故の相手の運転手は70才くらいの年輩者でした。
sentences.english: The other driver in the accident was a 70 year old elderly person.

meaningMnemonic: When a 限定 (limit) is applied to 販売 (selling), it’s a sort of exclusive sale or limited offer . 限定販売 is a sales strategy where companies limit the availability of their products to certain regions, stores, time frames, or club members.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 関西限定販売のアイスクリーム、やっと手に入れたんだ。
sentences.english: I finally got my hands on this ice cream, which is sold exclusively in the Kansai region.

sentences.japanese: え、これってハロウィンの季節だけの限定販売なの！？私、「限定販売」っていう言葉に弱いんだよね。
sentences.english: Wait, is this only on sale during the Halloween season? I'm a sucker for the phrase “limited-time offer.”

sentences.japanese: 寝台車付き特急の実物大型模型を買おうか迷っているんだけど、日本では三台のみの限定販売になるみたいなんだよね。
sentences.english: I'm considering buying a life-sized model of a limited express train with sleeper cars, but it seems that in Japan, only three units will be sold as a limited edition.

meaningMnemonic: At the extreme edge , which is just the extreme . 極端 means something is taken to the extreme without moderation, so it generally has a negative connotation.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: ちょっと嫌なことがあったからって会社を辞めるなんて、武井さんも極端ですねぇ！
sentences.english: Mr. Takei, you're being quite extreme by quitting the company just because something unpleasant happened, don't you think?

sentences.japanese: 年金ってさ、めっちゃ極端に言えば「生き残れたラッキーな人に対して、若い人にお金を出させる」仕組みでしょ？
sentences.english: When you put it in extreme terms, isn't pension basically a system where 'the lucky survivors' make the young people pay for it?

sentences.japanese: 私は制服って素晴らしいと思ってるんです。極端な話、皆が同じ服を着ることで、それぞれの中身の個性が際立つと思うんですよ。
sentences.english: I think uniforms are fantastic to be honest. In extreme terms, I believe that everyone wearing the same clothing makes their individual personalities stand out.

sentences.japanese: 君は奇跡を起こすことができるかもしれない。でも、僕は君には極端なことは避けてもらいたいんだよ。
sentences.english: You may be able to perform miracles, but I want you to avoid doing extreme things.

meaningMnemonic: Getting a position of employment means finding employment . 就職 means getting a job or starting employment , usually after finishing school. It refers to formally entering the workforce, not just casually picking up part-time work. You'll hear it a lot in phrases like 就職活動 (job hunting) or 就職先 (place of employment).
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 就職おめでとう！
sentences.english: Congratulations on finding a job!

sentences.japanese: 明日の夜、友達の就職祝いをします。
sentences.english: We're going to celebrate my friend's new job tomorrow night.

sentences.japanese: 卒業後、ちゃんと就職できるか不安なんです。
sentences.english: I am worried about whether I will be able to find a job after graduation.

sentences.japanese: 「いくつか就職の面接をしたんだけど、まだどこからも内定が出ないんだ。」「お互い大変だな。」
sentences.english: "I've had several job interviews, but I haven't received any job offers yet." "Join the club."

meaningMnemonic: You have prosper ed so much that light seems to shine forth from your every pore in a golden aura. With the wealth, fame, and admiration you have achieved, you are the walking embodiment of glory . 栄光 is commonly used in expressions like 過去の栄光 (past glory), referring to the great achievements or status that one had in the past.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 今回、勝利の栄光を手にしたのは、トーフグチームです！
sentences.english: The team that won a glorious victory this time is Team Tofugu!

sentences.japanese: あの芸人のネタ、『M1グランプリ』の栄光を勝ち取ったとは思えないクオリティだな。
sentences.english: That quality of that comedian's material makes it hard to believe they won the M-1 Grand Prix.

sentences.japanese: 「昔の栄光を語るヤクザほどミジメな者はない」ってビエトが言ってたよ。
sentences.english: Viet said, "There's no one more pathetic than a yakuza who talks about past glory."

meaningMnemonic: Step by step . If you take things step by step, you're moving up gradually , taking steps . 段々 is often used to describe gradual progress. But sometimes you'll see it used for terraced fields or buildings too, since they sorta resemble steps!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 私の日本語が段々うまくなっていると言ってもらえて、すごく嬉しいです。
sentences.english: I’m glad to hear that my Japanese is gradually getting better.

sentences.japanese: 山田さん、そこ段々になってるから気をつけて！
sentences.english: Mr. Yamada, be careful, the ground is stepped there!

sentences.japanese: この段々畑の絵、最初は好きじゃなかったけど、見てるうちに段々気に入ってきたんだよね。
sentences.english: At first, I didn't like this painting of the terraced fields, but as I kept looking at it, I gradually started to like it.

sentences.japanese: 段々雲行きが怪しくなってきました。
sentences.english: Gradually, things started to not look good.

meaningMnemonic: Take the middle route , half to the edge . You don't do anything the full way. Just to the middle. Just to the half. Not to the edge. This was really half finished and half assed of you.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The ぱ at the end is the only tricky part here since that isn't a common reading (or the one you learned before) for the kanji. Just think of your ol' Pa ( ぱ ), who is the biggest half-asser you know.

sentences.japanese: 今思うと、すごく中途半端なことをしてたと思います。
sentences.english: Thinking back now, I was doing it by halves.

sentences.japanese: 中途半端に物事を学んだとしても、それが全て無だになるわけじゃないよ。
sentences.english: Even when you learn something halfway, what you have learned won't all go in vain.

sentences.japanese: そういう中途半端な態度が一番ムカつくんだよ。
sentences.english: That kind of half-hearted attitude is what pisses me off the most.

sentences.japanese: 俺は中途半端な生き方をしてきたかもしれないけど、マフィアに入りたいって思ったことは一度もないよ。
sentences.english: My life may be incomplete, but I would've never dreamt of joining the mafia.

meaningMnemonic: You have hand and the noun version of 拭く (to wipe). Put the two together and you get a hand wipe ! お手拭き refers to a wet hand towel or wet napkin used for cleaning your hands, often provided at restaurants in Japan before a meal.
readingMnemonic: The reading for this uses all kun'yomi. So just put together the kun'yomis of 手 and 拭き (from the verb 拭く ) with an honorary お and you're good to go!

sentences.english: Oh, feel free to use this hand wipe!

sentences.english: When I sit down at a restaurant, I first wipe my hands with a hand wipe.

meaningMnemonic: You're so healthy it puts you at ease . That's your health ! So healthful, go you!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 健康に勝るものは何もないですよ。
sentences.english: Nothing is better than good health.

sentences.japanese: 健康のために水泳を始めました。
sentences.english: I started swimming for my health.

sentences.japanese: このウィルスは、健康な人にはほとんど心配いりません。
sentences.english: This virus rarely affects healthy people.

sentences.japanese: 会社側が負担する健康保険は、諸手当の中に含まれているのでしょうか。
sentences.english: Is company-paid health insurance included in the fringe benefits?

meaningMnemonic: You learned that 抜ける is "to fall out." If an interval of time falls out of you, you're totally spaced out. You won't learn anything and you'll become an idiot . 間抜け can refer to both a person who does something foolish and to the foolish actions themselves. It's often used to criticize dumb behavior.
readingMnemonic: The readings come from the ま reading of 間 and from 抜く .

sentences.japanese: オレ、間抜けだから、気づかなかったよ。言ってくれてありがとう。

sentences.japanese: 間抜けな返事をしてしまい、はずかしく思っています。
sentences.english: I feel ashamed of the stupid reply I sent.

sentences.japanese: アイツの間抜けヅラ、見た？
sentences.english: Did you see his dumb face?

sentences.japanese: 彼に間抜けな田舎者のお上りさんだと思われたくないの。
sentences.english: I don’t want him to think of me as a stupid country bumpkin.

meaningMnemonic: The not sleep symptom shows you have a disorder that involves not sleeping. That is insomnia .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 不眠症に悩まされています。
sentences.english: I'm suffering from insomnia.

sentences.japanese: 不眠症に効く薬を売ってください。
sentences.english: Please sell me medicine that is effective for insomnia.

sentences.japanese: 彼と仕事をするのがストレスで、不眠症になってしまいました。
sentences.english: Working with him is so stressful that I got insomnia.

meaningMnemonic: An alive alcohol shop is a place that serves a lot of alcohol. In Japan, these places are often izakaya . If you don't already know what an izakaya is, you can consider it to be a casual Japanese Style Bar . An izakaya is a pub or tavern where you can enjoy drinks and tasty bar food like yakitori and gyoza, usually at quite affordable prices. Cheers!
readingMnemonic: The readings here are all kun'yomi, but this is the first time you've seen the さか reading for 酒 , which rendaku then turns into ざか here. If you know what an izakaya is already, you can probably remember the reading, but if not here's a mnemonic to help: When you need recommendations for a good izakaya (a Japanese style bar ), you ask your friend Zacha ry ( ざか ). He knows all the best spots. You even call him Izakaya Zachary. He doesn't like that, but too bad. In your mind, Zachary will always be tied to Japanese style bars.

sentences.english: Do you have any recommendations for a good izakaya?

meaningMnemonic: This word comes from 任せる , but without the る on the end it's a noun. You also have the honorific お on the beginning, which is a clue that you're addressing someone else. So you're entrusting something to the person you're talking to, and this means leaving decisions to someone else . This is used a lot in restaurants, where it means chef's choice or simply omakase . In other words, you're leaving the choice of food to the chef. It can be used in other contexts, too, like if you leave your haircut up to your stylist or a flower arrangement up to the florist, or even if you follow the recommended program at the gym.
readingMnemonic: You learned this reading with the word 任せる , so I'll leave this one to you.

meaningMnemonic: The value is in various steps . meaningMnemonic: We all build up something in front of ourselves. It's the front we present to the world, the public behavior , public stance and social niceties that maintain harmony. 建前 is very important in Japan. For example, you might find yourself invited to an acquaintance's home out of courtesy, with the expectation that you’ll decline (also out of courtesy!). A host of a party may say "just bring yourself," but guests know this could be 建前 , and considering their own 建前 , they bring a small gift anyways.  People can also be reluctant to say "no" to things, like drinks with coworkers when they really want to go home, and may not to show it when they find situations inconvenient or unpleasant. So you might need some guesswork to peek behind the 建前 that people build up in front of themselves!

Use it to say a picture is hung on the wall, for example. 掛かる can also mean to be hooked , whether it's the picture hooked to the wall or a fish that happens to be caught on a hook. These uses are all intransitive, so you don't need a direct object them. A hint for this is that 掛かる ends with okurigana that rhyme with ある , and those kinds of verbs tend to be intransitive.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 掛ける , so as long as you know that you know this too.

sentences.english: I'd like to hang the clock here, but I'm not sure if it will hang right.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means belong so the verb vocab version is to belong to . 属する is a formal term for describing someone or something’s belonging to or being part of a group, category or classification.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji. This kanji is going to belong to you.

sentences.english: Whose group were you in when you were in grade four?

sentences.english: The starting month of the service will be the month in which the service start date belongs to. The service start date will be the day on which we confirm that the customer has received the SIM card.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means yield , and 屈む means to bend down or to crouch . After all, bending down and crouching are sort of like yielding to gravity, don’t you think? 屈む refers to the act of lowering your head or body, so it can also mean to duck or to squat depending on the context.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You always have to bend down to get into your car ga rage ( かが ) because you’re just too tall. You have to crouch just to get inside your car garage! Let’s hope you can find a bigger one someday.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means catch , so the verb vocab version means to catch or to grab . 捕まえる generally refers to the act of physically catching a person, animal, or object. By extension, you can also use it for things like grabbing a server's attention in a busy restaurant, tracking down an employee in a massive store to ask a question, or even catching a passing taxi on the street. Basically, if it takes effort to catch, 捕まえる works!
readingMnemonic: Like most verbs, this word uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you out: When police want to catch a criminal, they often take two car s ( つか ). By using two cars, cops can come at a suspect from multiple directions and block their escape routes, making them much easier to catch.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how 抜く means "to pull something out"? 抜ける describes something coming out of where it was, so it means to come out or to fall out . This can be used for air coming out of a balloon, hair falling out, or pages missing from a book. It also means passing through places or leaving a group you were a part of. To distinguish this word from 抜く , imagine a bunch of kale ( ける ) coming out of the ground on its own! Nobody pulled it out, it just came out by itself.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. Also, it is the same as 抜く .

sentences.japanese: 森を抜けると、そこには真っ青な海が広がっていました。

meaningMnemonic: When you tighten things up and bind things together, it's hard to separate them again. That's why this word is used to conclude or to enter into important agreements, like treaties and contracts. Note that this word is quite formal, which makes sense, given the contexts it’s usually used in.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means angry , the verb vocab version is to get angry .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You're starting to get angry about something. It's mostly this ok ra ( おこ ). It tastes terrible.

meaningMnemonic: This word is a combination of お腹 (belly) and 空く (to become empty). When your belly becomes empty, you're going to get hungry . お腹が空く is the most standard expression for saying you're hungry in Japanese. You'll typically use it in the past tense, like お腹が空いた . In conversation, it's common to drop the が , so you'll also hear people say things like お腹空いた！ when they're out with friends or family and want to grab a bite to eat. Note that it's often written in kana, either fully or partly, like お腹がすく .
readingMnemonic: お腹 uses the reading you learned with the vocabulary, but 空く is actually going to use a new reading here: すく . Here's a mnemonic to help you remember it: When you start to get hungry , you threaten to sue ( す ) the people around you for not feeding you. Some people just get hangry, but you get full-on litigious. You've threatened to sue your friends so many times now that they all habitually carry granola bars and trail mix to keep you from getting even the slightest bit peckish.

sentences.english: I'm getting hungry… Shall we take a lunch break?

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means astray and the verb vocab version is to go astray (because you don't just "to astray" now do you?). You can use it if you ever happen to get lost . Beyond physically getting lost, 迷う is also for times when you waver between different choices or hesitate to take a decisive step.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: If you are going to go astray , one way to do it would be to eat wayyyy too much mayo ( まよ ). I can't think of a worse way to go astray, personally.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means give so the verb vocab version is to give or to grant . sentences.english: First and foremost, I would like to express my sincere thanks for taking time out of your busy schedules to be here and for granting me the fantastic opportunity to give this presentation.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means renew , but the verb meaning is a little different. This means to grow late , to wear on , or to deepen . Think of it this way: you only renew stuff that's not new, after time has worn on a bit — your streaming subscriptions, your driver's license, your marriage vows. And with each renewal you feel the passage of time a little more deeply… You'll see 更ける more often in writing, usually in reference to night or autumn, as in 夜が更ける (the night grows late) and 秋が更ける (autumn deepens).
readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. As it starts to grow late , you turn into a foo l ( ふ ). You ever get increasingly delirious and giggly with friends as the night wears on? Yeah, you've been there. The later it gets, the more deeply foolish you become. What is that weird, late-night energy anyway?

meaningMnemonic: 隠す is "to hide something." 隠れる is to hide oneself or just to hide . You know this because when someone is hiding, it's rare ( れる ) for anyone else to find them. meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means long for , so the verb version is to long for and to yearn after .

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means tighten so the verb vocab version means to tighten , like a screw, or to tie, like a necktie or towel. 締める can also mean to wrap up when used in reference to a speech or some other occasion. In Japanese culture, people often 締める a situation with some shared action, like clapping in rhythm to end a celebration or having a final bowl of ramen to close out a night. You call it 締める because it's like you're tying off the event and giving it a sense of closure.
readingMnemonic: You go to tighten and to tie your captive up, and you realize you don't have anything to do it with. Then you see a sheep standing nearby. Okay. You take the shee p ( し ), pull its wool, and tie the sheep and your captive up together around a tree. Problem solved!

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means urge so the verb vocab version is to urge . meaningMnemonic: As usual, you can guess this is probably a verb because of the う sound on the end. The kanji means diagram , and if you've gone to the trouble of making a diagram, then you're likely trying to work toward some kind of goal. What is it that you're trying to plan ? Is your diagram helping you to take steps toward making it a reality? 図る is used when someone is taking steps or making an effort toward a goal, often in a somewhat formal or strategic sense. You'll see it in phrases like 解決を図る (attempt to resolve) or 改善を図る (aim for improvement).
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You're trying to work toward some big goal, so you've hired a hacker ( はか ) to help you. Whatever it is you're beginning to plan , you evidently felt you couldn't do it without a hacker. No one's accusing you of attempting to take steps toward anything nefarious, but… recruiting a hacker definitely doesn't scream "working for the good of my fellow man." Alternatively, you can remember this with the word 量る , which has the same reading. Just imagine you're meticulously measuring and weighing a bunch of stuff as you plan out how you're going to work toward your goal.

meaningMnemonic: When you get a position in some business , you’re considered working . 就業 is a formal word that can refer to both being employed and being at work for the day. It’s commonly used in kanji compounds, such as 就業時間 (working hours) and 就業規則 (employment regulations).
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 林さんの就業時間を教えてください。
sentences.english: What are Mr. Hayashi's working hours?

sentences.japanese: 就業規則についての話し合いをするために、 私たちは月一のペースで会っている。
sentences.english: We meet on a monthly basis to discuss employment regulations.

sentences.japanese: ハローワークに行っても、就業形態がパートのみの仕事しかすすめてもらえないんだよ。
sentences.english: When I go to Hello Work (employment service center), they only recommend part-time jobs to me.

sentences.japanese: 就業人口とは、労働力人口の中で、職業に就いて収入を得ている人の数のことです。 就業人口は、就業中の就業者と、何らかの事情により就業していない休業者に分けられます。
sentences.english: The working population refers to the number of individuals within the labor force who are employed and earning income. The working population can be further categorized into two groups: those who are actively working, and those who are on leave and not working due to various reasons.

meaningMnemonic: You have next year ( 来年 ), but then you do a year again . That's the year after next .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 再来年には景気もよくなっているでしょう。
sentences.english: By the year after next, the economy should have improved.

sentences.japanese: 再来年に日本の実家に帰るつもりです。
sentences.english: I plan to return to my family's home in Japan the year after next.

sentences.japanese: 再来年まで継続する二年契約を提案するべきではないでしょうか。
sentences.english: Shouldn't we propose a two-year contract that lasts until the year after next?

meaningMnemonic: The bathe clothes are clothes you wear to and from the bath. They're your yukata . 浴衣 originated as robes worn in a steam bath (that explains the kanji), but these days people mostly wear them at summer festivals or traditional Japanese inns. Be careful not to mix up 浴衣 with 着物 , which are much more formal and elaborate!
readingMnemonic: The reading is totally an exception. The reading comes from the meaning, though. Yukata = ゆかた .
